subtopic_detail: Severe lithium toxicity threshold and haemodialysis indication
stem:
A 62-year-old woman with bipolar I on lithium modified-release 900 mg nocte for 14 years presents with three days of unsteadiness, coarse tremor, and slurred speech. Her GP started perindopril 5 mg daily two weeks ago for stage 1 hypertension. She had gastroenteritis last week and drank little for 48 hours.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, oriented to place only, with horizontal nystagmus, dysarthria, hyperreflexia and bilateral coarse tremor. No focal weakness. Her last psychiatry review two months ago recorded a steady-state 12-hour trough lithium of 0.7 mmol/L on the current dose. Ambulance took bloods twenty minutes ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 14.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 82 six months ago), eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73m2, lithium 2.9 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.4-1.0)
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm, QTc 448 ms, no U waves
data_table.Medications: Lithium MR 900 mg nocte, perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold lithium, give intravenous normal saline at 200 mL/hour, and repeat lithium in 6 hours before deciding on further intervention
options.rationale: IV crystalloid alone is appropriate for mild toxicity (<1.5) or moderate toxicity with preserved renal function, but this patient has severe toxicity plus acute kidney injury from ACE-inhibitor plus volume depletion, so renal clearance cannot rescue her within the window before neurological deterioration. Would be correct if lithium were 1.6-2.4 with normal creatinine (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Withhold lithium and perindopril, commence intravenous crystalloid, and arrange urgent extracorporeal treatment (haemodialysis) via ICU and renal referral
options.rationale: EXTRIP workgroup and Australian toxicology guidance recommend haemodialysis for lithium concentration >4.0 in any patient, >2.5 with impaired kidney function or reduced consciousness or life-threatening features, or >2.5 not expected to fall below 1.0 within 36 hours. This patient meets the second criterion (2.9 with AKI and altered mental state) and the third (renal impairment blocks clearance). Intermittent haemodialysis is preferred; continuous renal replacement therapy is an acceptable alternative if unstable (Source: Poisons Information Centre; EXTRIP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally and observe with 4-hourly lithium concentrations on the medical ward
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not adsorb lithium; whole-bowel irrigation is considered for large modified-release ingestions but not for chronic toxicity from steady-state dosing. Ward-level observation misses the dialysis window in severe toxicity with AKI. Would never be correct for lithium (Source: Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Continue lithium at reduced dose of 450 mg nocte, cease perindopril, and repeat lithium concentration and creatinine in 48 hours in the community
options.rationale: Continuing any lithium with a 2.9 concentration risks worsening neurotoxicity and permanent cerebellar injury; community follow-up is unsafe for severe toxicity with altered consciousness. Would be correct only for stable therapeutic drift without symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol as a bolus to enhance urinary lithium excretion by alkalinisation
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation enhances elimination of weak acids (salicylate, phenobarbitone) but has no effect on lithium clearance, which is a small unionised cation reabsorbed with sodium in the proximal tubule. Volume repletion with saline is the correct first-line renal augmentation strategy. Would never be correct for lithium (Source: Poisons Information Centre; AMH).

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is graded by concentration and clinical features. Mild (1.5-2.5) presents with tremor, GI upset and mild ataxia and usually responds to withholding lithium plus IV crystalloid to restore volume and drive renal clearance. Moderate (2.5-3.5) or any concentration with altered consciousness, seizures, or arrhythmia is severe. EXTRIP haemodialysis criteria for the Australian setting are: any concentration >4.0, concentration >2.5 with impaired renal function or reduced conscious state or life-threatening features, or concentration >2.5 not expected to fall below 1.0 within 36 hours on saline alone. Chronic toxicity is more neurotoxic at any given concentration than acute overdose because tissue equilibration is already complete. Reversible AKI (ACE inhibitor plus dehydration plus NSAID triad) is the classical precipitant.
key_points: Haemodialysis threshold: >4.0 always; >2.5 with AKI, altered mental state, or arrhythmia
Perindopril + gastroenteritis + long-term lithium = classic chronic-on-therapeutic toxicity
Activated charcoal does not adsorb lithium; alkalinisation has no effect
SILENT (syndrome of irreversible lithium-effectuated neurotoxicity) can follow poorly-treated severe toxicity
Continuous renal replacement is acceptable when intermittent haemodialysis unavailable or patient unstable
explanation.pearls: In context: any lithium concentration above 2.5 mmol/L with either acute kidney injury, altered mental state, or arrhythmia mandates haemodialysis referral in Australian toxicology practice (Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26).

stem:
A 54-year-old woman with bipolar II maintained on lithium modified-release 800 mg nocte (last trough 0.72 mmol/L four months ago) attends her GP for review of stage 2 hypertension. She has been on amlodipine 10 mg daily but her home readings average 152/94. She is otherwise well, with normal renal function two months ago (creatinine 68 micromol/L).

The GP is considering adding a second agent and phones the community psychiatry team for advice. She takes no NSAIDs or other regular medications, and her weight is stable.

data_table.Bloods: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Medications: Lithium MR 800 mg nocte, amlodipine 10 mg daily

lead_in: Which second-line antihypertensive is most appropriate given her lithium therapy?

options.text: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily with lithium concentration checked at one week
options.rationale: Thiazides increase proximal tubular sodium and lithium reabsorption by inducing volume contraction, raising lithium concentration by around 25 to 40 percent within a week; concentration monitoring alone does not mitigate the risk if a safer alternative exists. Would be a second-choice option only if all others were contraindicated (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Perindopril 5 mg daily titrated to 10 mg with lithium concentration checked at one week
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors reduce renal lithium clearance especially in older adults and in volume depletion, and their effect is less predictable than the calcium-channel or beta-blocker class. Would be acceptable with weekly bloods only if calcium-channel and beta-blocker options were unsuitable (Source: AMH).

options.text: Indapamide 2.5 mg daily as a thiazide-like agent with less potassium loss
options.rationale: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic and behaves the same way as hydrochlorothiazide for lithium clearance; the potassium-sparing advantage does not offset the lithium interaction. Would never be first choice with lithium (Source: AMH).

options.text: Add a second calcium-channel or beta-blocker agent (for example bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily) as an alternative class with minimal lithium interaction
options.rationale: Beta-blockers and calcium-channel blockers do not meaningfully affect lithium concentration and are the preferred add-ons when combined therapy is needed alongside lithium. This preserves antihypertensive efficacy without triggering the thiazide, ACE-inhibitor, or ARB interactions that account for most avoidable lithium toxicity presentations to Australian EDs (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Irbesartan 150 mg daily as an ARB with fewer interactions than ACE inhibitors
options.rationale: ARBs share the ACE-inhibitor mechanism of reducing renal lithium clearance and have been implicated in lithium toxicity presentations at similar rates to ACE inhibitors; the class advantage is on cough, not on lithium interaction. Would be second-choice only when calcium-channel and beta-blocker options were unsuitable (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Lithium is renally cleared and shares proximal tubular handling with sodium. Any drug or state that reduces sodium delivery to the proximal tubule (thiazides, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, dehydration) increases lithium reabsorption and raises concentration. Beta-blockers and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers do not affect lithium handling. Australian Prescriber summarises the practical hierarchy: prefer beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker as second-line antihypertensive in a lithium-treated patient; if thiazide or renin-angiotensin blockade is clinically necessary, check lithium at day 5-7 and again at 2-4 weeks, and warn the patient about sick-day rules.
key_points: Thiazides raise lithium by 25-40 percent within a week
ACE inhibitors and ARBs both reduce lithium clearance
NSAIDs (except aspirin) raise lithium by 15-30 percent
Beta-blockers and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are lithium-neutral
Sick-day rules apply to any dehydrating illness on lithium
explanation.pearls: In context: when adding a second antihypertensive to a lithium-treated patient, calcium-channel blockers or beta-blockers are the interaction-neutral choice; thiazides and renin-angiotensin blockers demand explicit lithium monitoring within a week (AMH; Australian Prescriber).

stem:
A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 500 mg nocte for four years. He presents to ED with two weeks of worsening abdominal distension, three days without a bowel motion, and one episode of vomiting last night. His outpatient team started paroxetine 20 mg daily eight weeks ago for comorbid depression. He has been on macrogol 13 g daily for constipation, which he takes intermittently.

He is comfortable at rest but obviously distended, with generalised tenderness and no peritonism, and bowel sounds are sluggish. A rectal exam reveals an empty rectal vault.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 106, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Bloods: White cell count 8.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 5.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), CRP 22 mg/L (<5), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (<2.0), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 84 micromol/L
data_table.Abdominal x-ray: Massively dilated large bowel loops with faecal loading to the caecum; no free gas
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 500 mg nocte, paroxetine 20 mg daily, macrogol 13 g PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase macrogol to 26 g daily, add senna 15 mg nocte, keep clozapine at current dose, and reassess bowels in 48 hours in the community
options.rationale: This is severe clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility with radiological subacute obstruction and vomiting; outpatient laxative escalation misses the highest-mortality complication of clozapine (paralytic ileus and toxic megacolon carry case-fatality up to 15-28 percent). Would be reasonable only for asymptomatic constipation without distension or vomiting (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Admit for nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, nasogastric decompression, cease paroxetine and macrogol, withhold clozapine pending surgical review, and start a stimulant plus osmotic laxative combination once obstruction is excluded
options.rationale: Symptomatic clozapine-induced GI hypomotility with vomiting and radiological obstruction is a surgical emergency and requires bowel rest, decompression and IV fluids; paroxetine has additional anticholinergic burden and worsens transit. Clozapine is temporarily withheld (48-hour rule applies for restart), and stimulant plus osmotic laxatives are the recommended combination once mechanical obstruction is excluded on imaging or surgical review. Note the parallel-grammar break: this option lives on the acute-surgical axis rather than the outpatient-laxative axis, matching the disease severity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Australian Prescriber).

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 250 mg nocte immediately and continue current bowel regimen without further imaging or admission
options.rationale: Halving clozapine without inpatient decompression fails to relieve the acute distension and vomiting; abrupt large dose reduction also risks rebound psychosis and does not restore transit fast enough. Dose reduction alone would be appropriate only when transit has recovered (Source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Give a soap-suds enema on the ward and discharge with dietary fibre advice and a follow-up call at 24 hours
options.rationale: An enema does not address proximal colonic hypomotility (the caecum is loaded) and dietary fibre worsens distension in established hypomotility. Discharge misses the surgical monitoring required for evolving obstruction. Would be inadequate for radiological obstruction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start metoclopramide 10 mg intravenously three times daily to accelerate transit while continuing clozapine and outpatient laxatives
options.rationale: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that adds extrapyramidal and QT-prolongation burden on top of clozapine and does not act on the colon; prokinetic agents that act on the colon (prucalopride) are second-line after decompression and laxative combination. Metoclopramide plus clozapine also raises neuroleptic malignant syndrome risk. Would never be first-line (Source: AMH; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility is the single largest cause of clozapine-related mortality, exceeding agranulocytosis by several-fold in Australian pharmacovigilance data. Mechanism is combined anticholinergic (M2, M3) and serotonergic block on the enteric nervous system. Concurrent anticholinergic drugs (tricyclics, paroxetine, oxybutynin), opioids, and dehydration all magnify the risk. RANZCP and Maudsley recommend routine prophylactic laxatives at clozapine initiation (osmotic first-line; add stimulant when >250 mg/day). Symptomatic hypomotility with distension, vomiting, or absent bowel motions warrants admission for bowel rest, decompression, imaging, and surgical review because deterioration to ileus and toxic megacolon can be rapid.
key_points: Clozapine GI hypomotility case-fatality up to 15-28 percent when it progresses to ileus
Prophylactic laxatives from initiation; stimulant plus osmotic above 250 mg/day
Anticholinergic co-prescribing (paroxetine, tricyclics, oxybutynin) magnifies risk
Symptomatic hypomotility = admission, imaging, surgical review
Clozapine withhold plus 48-hour rule for retitration once transit restored
explanation.pearls: In context: constipation is the deadliest adverse effect of clozapine in Australian practice; symptomatic hypomotility with vomiting or radiological loading always earns admission, not outpatient laxative escalation (Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

stem:
A 28-year-old woman with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is 24 days into clozapine titration and reached 250 mg nocte five days ago. She attends the clozapine clinic for her routine review. She reports intermittent chest heaviness on climbing stairs since yesterday and mild ankle swelling this morning. She has felt more tired than usual for four days.

She has been afebrile at home. Weekly bloods have been within limits and troponin and CRP were normal at baseline.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: JVP 5 cm above sternal angle, bibasal fine crackles, faint S3 gallop, trace pedal oedema
data_table.Bloods: Neutrophils 4.6 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), CRP 62 mg/L (<5), troponin I 240 ng/L (<26), eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (<0.5)
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia rate 118, non-specific T-wave flattening in V4-V6, no ST elevation
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 250 mg nocte (day 24 of titration), OCP

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue clozapine, repeat troponin and CRP in 48 hours, and arrange outpatient cardiology review within a week
options.rationale: Titration-window troponin rise plus CRP rise plus tachycardia plus new heart-failure signs meets the composite criterion for probable clozapine-induced myocarditis; continuing the drug risks progression to fulminant disease. Would be appropriate only for isolated CRP rise below 100 with troponin still within range (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately, admit for cardiac monitoring, arrange urgent transthoracic echocardiogram and cardiology review, and do not rechallenge
options.rationale: During the first six to eight weeks of clozapine, troponin above twice the upper limit of normal or new cardiac symptoms combined with CRP elevation trigger immediate cessation, admission, echocardiography, and cardiology review. Australian pharmacovigilance recognises clozapine-induced myocarditis at incidence around 1 per 100 initiations with peak onset days 14-21. Rechallenge is generally contraindicated after confirmed myocarditis because recurrence rates approach 30 percent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Australian Prescriber).

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 100 mg nocte and add bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily to manage the tachycardia
options.rationale: Dose reduction without cessation fails to arrest ongoing myocardial inflammation, and beta-blockade masks the tachycardia (an early warning sign) without treating the underlying process. Would never be correct for suspected clozapine myocarditis (Source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Continue clozapine, start empirical intravenous ceftriaxone for suspected community-acquired pneumonia, and reassess symptoms in 24 hours
options.rationale: No focal chest signs or CXR abnormality has been demonstrated; empirical antibiotics for CAP without evidence miss the titration-window myocarditis pattern and delay definitive cardiology assessment. Would be correct only when clinical or radiological pneumonia was established (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Continue clozapine, defer troponin repeat, and refer for holter monitoring within two weeks
options.rationale: Deferring investigation in a symptomatic patient with a troponin nine times upper limit of normal is unsafe; holter monitoring addresses arrhythmia not myocarditis, and the diagnostic modality is echocardiography plus cardiac MRI, not ambulatory rhythm capture. Would never be correct here (Source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis is a titration-window (typically day 10-30) hypersensitivity phenomenon presenting with tachycardia, fatigue, mild dyspnoea, fever, eosinophilia and troponin/CRP rise. Australian clozapine clinics screen with baseline troponin, CRP, ECG, and echocardiogram, then weekly troponin and CRP through the first four weeks. A troponin above twice the upper limit of normal, or new cardiac symptoms with CRP rise, triggers immediate cessation and cardiology review. Fulminant cases develop cardiogenic shock over 24-48 hours; missed cases contribute to the small excess cardiovascular mortality in early clozapine treatment. Rechallenge is generally contraindicated after confirmed myocarditis but occasionally attempted in specialist centres with intensive monitoring after full recovery.
key_points: Peak onset days 14-21 of titration
Screening: baseline echocardiogram, weekly troponin and CRP first four weeks
Cease at troponin >2x ULN or new cardiac symptoms with CRP rise
Cardiac MRI is the definitive diagnostic modality
Recurrence on rechallenge approaches 30 percent
explanation.pearls: In context: any troponin above twice the upper limit of normal or new cardiac symptom with CRP rise in the first six weeks of clozapine is myocarditis until proven otherwise, and mandates immediate cessation plus cardiology admission (Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

subtopic_detail: Severe neutropenia response and GCSF eligibility
stem:
A 41-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg nocte for six years with monthly blood monitoring under the Clopine Connect program. Today's routine bloods return with total white cell count 2.4 and neutrophils 0.9. He is asymptomatic, afebrile, and attends work at his supported employment placement. Last month's neutrophils were 3.1.

He takes no other regular medications. The clinic phones him to attend today and arranges a repeat FBC as per protocol, which returns 90 minutes later with the same result confirmed.

data_table.Bloods: White cell count 2.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 0.9 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), lymphocytes 1.2 x10^9/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 148 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Continue clozapine at full dose with twice-weekly FBC until neutrophils return above 2.0
options.rationale: Neutrophils below 1.0 meet the Clopine Connect red-zone threshold and clozapine must be ceased, not continued. Twice-weekly bloods without cessation risks further fall to critical levels and severe infection. Would never be correct at ANC <1.0 (Source: Clopine Connect protocol; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately, notify the Clopine Connect coordinator, arrange daily FBC, admit for haematology review, and add prophylactic filgrastim (GCSF) if neutrophils fall below 0.5 or fail to recover within 3 days
options.rationale: Neutrophils below 1.0 is the red-zone in the Australian clozapine haematology protocol, requiring immediate cessation, daily FBC, and haematology review. GCSF is not routine at ANC 0.5-1.0 but is added if the ANC falls below 0.5 (severe neutropenia) or fails to recover within a few days, and shortens the duration of neutropenia. Rechallenge is generally not permitted after a red-zone episode without haematology and treating psychiatrist sign-off in a specialist framework (Source: Clopine Connect protocol; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 200 mg nocte and start empirical piperacillin-tazobactam for febrile neutropenia
options.rationale: The patient is not febrile so febrile-neutropenia protocol does not apply; dose reduction without cessation is insufficient at ANC <1.0. Would be correct only if febrile with ANC <0.5 (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Continue clozapine, add lithium 250 mg daily to raise neutrophil count, and repeat FBC in one week
options.rationale: Lithium can raise neutrophil count via GCSF induction and has been used adjunctively in benign ethnic neutropenia, but is not the standard Australian response to red-zone clozapine neutropenia and does not permit continued clozapine at ANC <1.0. Would never substitute for cessation and haematology review (Source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Cease clozapine and permanently list him as ineligible for clozapine rechallenge nationally
options.rationale: Rechallenge is restricted and requires specialist framework, but is not universally prohibited after a single red-zone episode; benign ethnic neutropenia protocols and haematology-supervised rechallenge exist. Would over-restrict compared to Clopine Connect guidance (Source: Clopine Connect protocol).

explanation.summary: Clozapine haematological monitoring in Australia uses coloured-zone thresholds. Green (ANC >2.0 and WCC >3.5) is normal, allowing routine monthly bloods. Amber (ANC 1.5-2.0 or WCC 3.0-3.5) requires increased frequency (twice weekly) and often does not require cessation. Red (ANC <1.5 or WCC <3.0) requires immediate cessation, daily FBC, and haematology review; ANC <0.5 is severe (agranulocytosis) and warrants GCSF. Peak risk is in the first 18 weeks of treatment with declining incidence thereafter, but late presentations still occur and life-long monthly monitoring is standard. Benign ethnic neutropenia is a recognised carve-out with lower ANC thresholds applied under specialist supervision.
key_points: Red zone ANC <1.5 = cease + daily FBC + haematology review
Severe neutropenia ANC <0.5 = add GCSF (filgrastim)
Peak incidence first 18 weeks; monitoring is monthly life-long thereafter
Rechallenge is restricted but not universally banned after red-zone
Benign ethnic neutropenia has specialist-supervised alternative thresholds
explanation.pearls: In context: an absolute neutrophil count below 1.5 x10^9/L on clozapine is the red-zone trigger for immediate cessation and haematology review, and GCSF is added only when the count falls below 0.5 or recovery stalls (Clopine Connect; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

subtopic_detail: TGA and RANZCP restrictions in pregnancy-capable women
stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a first manic episode has responded well to olanzapine 15 mg nocte in the inpatient unit and is planning discharge. The inpatient consultant plans mood-stabiliser maintenance. She has one long-term partner, is using the combined oral contraceptive pill, and states clearly she does not want children in the next five years. Her routine bloods, LFTs, TFTs and renal function are within normal limits.

She asks specifically about valproate because a family member takes it and manages well.

data_table.Bloods: LFTs, TFTs, U&Es, FBC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding valproate as maintenance therapy?

options.text: Prescribe valproate as first-line maintenance given her stated intention not to conceive in the next five years
options.rationale: Under the TGA-mandated valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program (updated 2023), valproate must not be used in females of reproductive potential unless alternatives are ineffective or not tolerated, regardless of stated intention or contraception, because the pooled foetal-anticonvulsant-syndrome risk is around 10 percent malformation and up to 30-40 percent neurodevelopmental impairment. Would be inappropriate here (Source: TGA Valproate PPP; RANZCP; AMH).

options.text: Recommend lithium as first-line maintenance for bipolar I after pre-conception counselling and baseline renal, thyroid and parathyroid workup
options.rationale: For bipolar I maintenance in a pregnancy-capable woman, lithium is the first-line mood stabiliser under RANZCP guidance because valproate is restricted by the TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program and carbamazepine has significant teratogenicity plus enzyme-induction complications with the OCP. Baseline renal, thyroid, and parathyroid workup precedes lithium initiation. Note this option lives on the drug-class-choice axis rather than the counselling-only axis, so parallel-grammar shift is deliberate (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH).

options.text: Prescribe valproate provided she enrols in the Pregnancy Prevention Program, uses two forms of contraception, and signs an annual risk-acknowledgement form
options.rationale: The Pregnancy Prevention Program permits valproate in a pregnancy-capable woman only when alternatives (lithium, second-generation antipsychotics, lamotrigine) are ineffective or not tolerated; enrolment plus contraception does not remove that threshold requirement. Would be correct only after documented failure of alternatives (Source: TGA Valproate PPP).

options.text: Prescribe carbamazepine as it does not carry the same teratogenic restrictions as valproate
options.rationale: Carbamazepine has confirmed teratogenicity (neural tube defects around 1 percent, other malformations 3-4 percent) and reduces combined-OCP contraceptive efficacy via CYP3A4 induction; it is not preferred over lithium in a pregnancy-capable woman with bipolar I. Would be correct only in specific niche indications after specialist review (Source: AMH; RANZCP).

options.text: Continue olanzapine monotherapy as long-term maintenance without adding a mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Olanzapine monotherapy is a reasonable maintenance option in some patients but carries substantial metabolic burden and less relapse-prevention evidence than lithium in bipolar I; RANZCP still positions lithium as first-line maintenance for bipolar I. Would be acceptable only when lithium is contraindicated or refused after informed counselling (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Valproate in pregnancy carries the highest teratogenic burden of any commonly used mood stabiliser: around 10 percent risk of major malformations (spina bifida, cardiac defects, cleft palate, hypospadias) and up to 30-40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment including reduced IQ, autism spectrum disorder, and ADHD. The TGA introduced a Pregnancy Prevention Program (updated 2023) requiring specialist prescribing, annual risk acknowledgement, and documented contraception; valproate is contraindicated in females of reproductive potential unless alternatives are ineffective or not tolerated. RANZCP positions lithium as first-line maintenance for bipolar I; lamotrigine is first-line for bipolar II depression-predominant illness; second-generation antipsychotics are alternatives. Pre-conception counselling should occur at diagnosis, not at pregnancy planning.
key_points: Valproate major malformation rate around 10 percent, neurodevelopmental impairment up to 30-40 percent
TGA PPP restricts valproate in females of reproductive potential regardless of stated intention
Lithium is first-line maintenance for bipolar I under RANZCP guidance
Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4 and reduces OCP efficacy plus teratogenic
Pre-conception counselling occurs at diagnosis, not at pregnancy planning
explanation.pearls: In context: the TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program prohibits first-line valproate in any pregnancy-capable woman with bipolar disorder regardless of contraception status, unless alternatives are documented ineffective or intolerable (TGA; RANZCP).

subtopic_detail: HLA-B*15:02 screening in Han Chinese ancestry
stem:
A 32-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder has recurrent affective episodes despite olanzapine plus escitalopram. His treating psychiatrist is considering carbamazepine as an adjunctive mood stabiliser. He was born in Melbourne to Han Chinese parents and both grandparents on each side are from mainland China. He has no personal or family history of adverse drug reactions.

His LFTs, U&Es and FBC are within normal limits. The team asks about safety screening before initiation.

data_table.Bloods: LFTs, U&Es, FBC within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg nocte, escitalopram 20 mg mane

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pre-initiation step?

options.text: Test HLA-B*15:02 and, if positive, avoid carbamazepine (and oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, and lamotrigine as a related class risk)
options.rationale: TGA product information and Australian Prescriber recommend HLA-B*15:02 genotyping in patients of Han Chinese, Thai, Malay, Filipino, Indonesian, or South Asian ancestry before starting carbamazepine because HLA-B*15:02 carries a relative risk of around 100 for carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN. A positive result is a contraindication and extends to structurally related aromatic antiepileptics (oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) which carry weaker but real cross-reactivity risk (Source: TGA PI Carbamazepine; Australian Prescriber; AMH).

options.text: Proceed with carbamazepine at standard titration; HLA-B*15:02 screening is routine only after a first suspected hypersensitivity reaction
options.rationale: Reactive genotyping (after a reaction) misses the primary preventive opportunity; prospective genotyping in high-risk ancestries is the Australian standard and has been cost-effective in modelled analyses. Would never be correct in a Han Chinese patient (Source: TGA PI Carbamazepine; Australian Prescriber).

options.text: Test HLA-B*57:01 to exclude carbamazepine hypersensitivity risk
options.rationale: HLA-B*57:01 is the abacavir hypersensitivity marker, not the carbamazepine SJS marker. Testing the wrong allele misses the actual risk. Would never be correct (Source: TGA; AMH).

options.text: Substitute sodium valproate at initiation as it has no SJS/TEN risk
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is not restricted by HLA-B*15:02 but carries its own risks (hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity) and is not the pharmacological equivalent of carbamazepine for this indication; the appropriate step is genotype-directed decision-making, not automatic substitution. Would be one of several alternatives if genotype was positive (Source: AMH).

options.text: Perform an oral carbamazepine challenge under monitored observation to assess for early rash
options.rationale: Provocation testing for SJS is unsafe and not part of any Australian guideline; SJS/TEN can appear 1-4 weeks after exposure and cannot be excluded by an acute challenge. Would never be correct (Source: TGA PI Carbamazepine).

explanation.summary: Carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis is strongly linked to HLA-B*15:02 in populations of Han Chinese, Thai, Malay, Filipino, Indonesian and South Asian ancestry, where allele frequency reaches 10-15 percent. The relative risk in carriers is approximately 100, and prospective genotyping followed by avoidance in carriers has eliminated most cases in Taiwan. TGA product information and Australian Prescriber recommend genotyping before initiation in ancestries where the allele is common. A positive genotype contraindicates carbamazepine and related aromatic antiepileptics (oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) which share partial cross-reactivity. HLA-A*31:01 is a separate marker associated with carbamazepine-induced hypersensitivity in European populations and is a lower-magnitude signal.
key_points: HLA-B*15:02: prospective genotyping in Han Chinese, Thai, Malay, Filipino, Indonesian, South Asian ancestry
Positive result contraindicates carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine
HLA-A*31:01 is a European-population marker (lower magnitude)
HLA-B*57:01 belongs to abacavir, not carbamazepine
SJS/TEN onset typically 1-4 weeks after exposure
explanation.pearls: In context: in a patient of Han Chinese ancestry, HLA-B*15:02 genotyping before carbamazepine is mandatory under TGA product information, and a positive result contraindicates the whole aromatic antiepileptic class (TGA; Australian Prescriber).

subtopic_detail: Lamotrigine dose adjustment when co-prescribed with valproate
stem:
A 38-year-old man with bipolar II is being started on lamotrigine for depression-predominant maintenance after inadequate response to quetiapine. He is already on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for a longstanding seizure disorder (managed by neurology) with a valproate concentration of 480 micromol/L. He has no personal or family history of rash or drug hypersensitivity, no HLA testing done, and takes no other regular medications.

He is Caucasian, weighs 78 kg, and is a non-smoker.

data_table.Bloods: LFTs, U&Es within normal limits; valproate concentration 480 micromol/L (therapeutic 350-700)
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily (500 mg BD)

lead_in: Which lamotrigine titration schedule is most appropriate?

options.text: Start lamotrigine 25 mg daily and increase to 100 mg over 4 weeks (standard mood-stabiliser titration)
options.rationale: Standard titration is for lamotrigine monotherapy or with enzyme-inducers; with concurrent valproate the standard schedule doubles the exposure and increases SJS/TEN risk. Would be correct only in the absence of valproate or enzyme-inducers (Source: AMH; TGA PI Lamotrigine).

options.text: Start lamotrigine 25 mg every second day for 2 weeks, then 25 mg daily for 2 weeks, then increase in 25-50 mg fortnightly increments up to a maintenance target of 100-200 mg daily
options.rationale: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles lamotrigine plasma concentrations; the co-prescription schedule under AMH and TGA product information halves both the starting dose and increment size (25 mg alternate days for 2 weeks, then 25 mg daily for 2 weeks, then slow fortnightly increases). Maintenance dose is typically 100-200 mg daily when combined with valproate, compared with 200-400 mg on monotherapy. Slow titration is the strongest modifiable factor reducing SJS/TEN risk (Source: AMH; TGA PI Lamotrigine; Australian Prescriber).

options.text: Start lamotrigine 50 mg daily and increase to 200 mg over 2 weeks to shorten time to therapeutic effect
options.rationale: Accelerated titration significantly raises SJS/TEN risk; the whole point of the slow schedule is to reduce that risk. Would never be correct (Source: TGA PI Lamotrigine).

options.text: Cease valproate first, then start lamotrigine at standard monotherapy dose from day one
options.rationale: Ceasing valproate risks breakthrough seizures in a patient with established seizure control and is not required to start lamotrigine; dose-adjusted co-prescription is standard neurology-psychiatry practice. Would never be correct here (Source: AMH).

options.text: Start lamotrigine 25 mg daily and double the dose weekly to reach 200 mg over 4 weeks with prophylactic prednisolone cover for rash risk
options.rationale: Weekly doubling is faster than the co-prescription protocol; prophylactic steroids do not prevent SJS/TEN and mask early inflammatory warning signs. Would never be correct (Source: TGA PI Lamotrigine).

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis is dose-and-titration dependent. Valproate inhibits UGT1A4 glucuronidation and roughly doubles lamotrigine plasma concentrations, so the co-prescription titration schedule halves both starting dose and rate of increment: 25 mg alternate days for 2 weeks, then 25 mg daily for 2 weeks, then fortnightly 25-50 mg increases up to a maintenance target of 100-200 mg daily. Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin) accelerate lamotrigine clearance and require higher maintenance doses (300-500 mg daily). The combined oral contraceptive also induces lamotrigine clearance and lamotrigine concentrations can fall 30-50 percent during the active pill weeks, rising back during the pill-free interval; concentration monitoring may be needed. Any new rash in the first 8 weeks warrants immediate cessation.
key_points: Valproate doubles lamotrigine concentration - halve starting dose and increments
Co-prescription maintenance target 100-200 mg daily (vs 200-400 mg monotherapy)
Enzyme-inducers require 300-500 mg daily maintenance
COC induces lamotrigine clearance; concentrations rise in pill-free week
New rash in first 8 weeks: immediate cessation
explanation.pearls: In context: with concurrent valproate the lamotrigine starting dose is 25 mg alternate days for 2 weeks and the maintenance target is 100-200 mg daily, half the monotherapy schedule (TGA Product Information; AMH).

subtopic_detail: Washout period switching from tranylcypromine to fluoxetine
stem:
A 47-year-old woman with treatment-resistant depression previously trialled sertraline, venlafaxine, and mirtazapine without response. She has been on tranylcypromine 20 mg BD for six months with partial response and troublesome insomnia and postural symptoms. Her psychiatrist and she agree to switch to fluoxetine, which has not been trialled.

Her last dose of tranylcypromine will be tomorrow morning.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg (lying), 96/58 mmHg (standing at 1 minute), HR 82

lead_in: What is the most appropriate switch protocol?

options.text: Cease tranylcypromine, wait 14 days as a washout, then commence fluoxetine
options.rationale: AMH and Therapeutic Guidelines specify a 14-day washout after ceasing an irreversible non-selective MAOI (tranylcypromine, phenelzine) before starting a serotonergic drug, to allow monoamine oxidase enzyme regeneration and prevent serotonin syndrome. Fluoxetine has a long half-life and would layer onto residual MAOI activity if started earlier, producing potentially fatal hyperthermic serotonin toxicity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH).

options.text: Cross-taper tranylcypromine and fluoxetine over 2 weeks with overlapping doses
options.rationale: Overlap of an irreversible MAOI and any SSRI is contraindicated; cross-taper is the standard method for switching between SSRIs but is unsafe for MAOI transitions. Would never be correct (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease tranylcypromine and commence fluoxetine after 5 days, matching the 5 half-life rule
options.rationale: The washout period for irreversible MAOIs is defined by enzyme regeneration (~14 days) not by drug half-life. A 5-day interval is unsafe. Would never be correct (Source: AMH).

options.text: Cease tranylcypromine and commence fluoxetine immediately at 10 mg with cyproheptadine cover for serotonin risk
options.rationale: Cyproheptadine is a treatment for established serotonin syndrome, not a prophylactic agent enabling immediate MAOI-SSRI overlap. Would never be correct (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease tranylcypromine, wait 5 weeks, then commence fluoxetine (matching the fluoxetine-to-MAOI washout in the opposite direction)
options.rationale: The 5-week wait applies in the opposite direction (fluoxetine to MAOI) because fluoxetine and its active metabolite have a combined half-life of several weeks. From MAOI to fluoxetine the wait is only the MAOI enzyme regeneration time of 14 days. Would over-delay treatment (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: MAOI switch protocols are asymmetric. Switching FROM an irreversible non-selective MAOI (tranylcypromine, phenelzine) TO any serotonergic drug requires a 14-day washout to allow monoamine oxidase enzyme regeneration. Switching TO an MAOI FROM most serotonergic drugs requires a 5-day washout, or 5 weeks after fluoxetine because of its long-half-life active metabolite norfluoxetine. Overlapping MAOI plus SSRI/SNRI can precipitate life-threatening serotonin syndrome (hyperthermia, autonomic instability, neuromuscular hyperactivity) requiring ICU-level care. Moclobemide is a reversible selective MAO-A inhibitor with shorter (typically 24-48 hour) washout requirements before or after serotonergic switching but still requires care.
key_points: Irreversible MAOI -> serotonergic drug: 14-day washout
Most SSRIs/SNRIs -> irreversible MAOI: 5-day washout
Fluoxetine -> irreversible MAOI: 5-week washout (long half-life metabolite)
Moclobemide: 24-48 hour washout in either direction
Serotonin syndrome from overlap: hyperthermia, clonus, autonomic instability
explanation.pearls: In context: switching from tranylcypromine to any serotonergic drug requires a 14-day drug-free washout to permit MAO enzyme regeneration; the wait is asymmetric with the 5-week fluoxetine washout in the opposite direction (AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

stem:
A 68-year-old woman on venlafaxine 225 mg XR daily for eight years for treatment-resistant depression is admitted to an orthopaedic ward with a prosthetic knee joint infection. Empirical piperacillin-tazobactam is started, then switched on culture and sensitivities to linezolid 600 mg BD by infectious diseases 36 hours ago. Her venlafaxine has been continued.

On the morning ward round she is agitated, restless, and shivering. She has bilateral lower limb rigidity that is greater than upper limbs, and inducible clonus at the ankles.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 168/98 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 96%, temperature 39.2
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, mydriasis, hyperreflexia (4+) lower limbs, inducible ankle clonus (>5 beats), tremor upper limbs, bowel sounds hyperactive
data_table.Bloods: CK 620 U/L (<170), WCC 11.2 x10^9/L, CRP 84 mg/L, U&Es and LFTs otherwise normal
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine XR 225 mg daily (last dose this morning), linezolid 600 mg BD (day 2), paracetamol 1 g QID PRN, oxycodone 5 mg 6-hourly PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease linezolid and venlafaxine, commence intravenous fluids and active cooling, give benzodiazepine (midazolam 2 mg IV) for agitation, and consult ICU and infectious diseases for alternative antibiotic
options.rationale: Linezolid is a reversible weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor and precipitates serotonin toxicity when combined with SSRIs, SNRIs, or MAOIs; features here (clonus, hyperreflexia lower > upper, mydriasis, agitation, autonomic instability, hyperthermia 39.2) satisfy the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria. Management is cessation of both offending agents, supportive care, benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, active cooling, and IV fluids; cyproheptadine is second-line if not improving. Alternative antibiotic must be sourced through infectious diseases (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Poisons Information Centre; AMH).

options.text: Cease linezolid only, continue venlafaxine, give paracetamol 1 g and reassess in 4 hours
options.rationale: Ongoing venlafaxine plus residual linezolid MAO inhibition continues to drive serotonin toxicity for at least 24 hours after linezolid cessation; paracetamol does not treat neurogenic hyperthermia and delays definitive cooling. Would never be correct (Source: Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Give bromocriptine and dantrolene for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: NMS presents with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and hypoactive bowel sounds, typically in the context of dopamine antagonist exposure or withdrawal of a dopamine agonist. This patient has clonus, hyperreflexia and hyperactive bowel sounds (serotonergic pattern) with no antipsychotic; bromocriptine plus dantrolene is not indicated. Would be correct if the picture were NMS after antipsychotic (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Give physostigmine for anticholinergic toxidrome
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxidrome presents with dry warm flushed skin, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention and mumbling delirium without clonus or hyperreflexia; this patient is diaphoretic with hyperactive bowel sounds and clonus. Physostigmine is misdirected and can precipitate seizures. Would never be correct here (Source: Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Continue both linezolid and venlafaxine, add clonidine for hypertension, and paracetamol for temperature
options.rationale: Continuing both offending drugs allows progressive multi-organ dysfunction; symptomatic BP and temperature control fails to address the underlying serotonergic excess. Would never be correct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and anticholinergic toxidrome share hyperthermia and altered mental state but discriminate by neuromuscular and bowel-sound pattern. Serotonin toxicity has clonus (especially inducible ankle clonus, spontaneous, or ocular), hyperreflexia predominantly in lower limbs, mydriasis, diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds, and rapid onset after a serotonergic drug or interaction. Hunter criteria have around 84 percent sensitivity and 97 percent specificity for serotonergic drug toxicity. NMS is bradykinetic lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, hypoactive bowel sounds, evolves over days, and follows dopamine antagonist exposure. Anticholinergic toxidrome is dry, red, absent bowel sounds and urinary retention. Linezolid is a reversible weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor and is the most common inpatient antibiotic implicated in serotonin toxicity.
key_points: Hunter criteria: clonus (spontaneous, inducible, or ocular) with other features
Serotonin syndrome: hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, hypoactive bowel sounds, dopamine antagonist context
Anticholinergic: dry hot flushed, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention
Linezolid + SSRI/SNRI is a recognised inpatient interaction pair
explanation.pearls: In context: inducible ankle clonus plus lower-limb hyperreflexia plus hyperactive bowel sounds in a patient on a serotonergic drug and linezolid is serotonin toxicity, not NMS or anticholinergic toxidrome (Poisons Information Centre; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

stem:
A 27-year-old woman is brought to ED by ambulance two hours after ingestion of approximately 50 amitriptyline 50 mg tablets with alcohol. Ambulance also found empty diazepam packets at the scene. She is now drowsy with pupils 5 mm reactive, warm dry skin, and hyperactive bowel sounds are absent.

Her partner reports she started amitriptyline three weeks ago for chronic pain.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), pH 7.30, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia rate 128, QRS 128 ms, terminal R in aVR >3 mm, no ST elevation, QTc 512 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate specific therapy?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol (100 mL of 8.4 percent) as a bolus with repeat FBC, ECG and blood gas in 10 minutes, aiming for QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.45-7.55
options.rationale: TCA cardiotoxicity is a fast-sodium-channel blockade; QRS above 100 ms and terminal R in aVR above 3 mm are Australian toxicology thresholds for sodium bicarbonate boluses (1-2 mmol/kg, or 100 mmol as a starting dose in an adult), aiming for QRS narrowing and arterial pH around 7.45-7.55. Repeat boluses as needed. This addresses the highest short-term mortality risk (ventricular arrhythmia and cardiogenic shock). Note this option is on the specific-antidote axis while other options are on symptomatic or contraindicated axes (Source: Poisons Information Centre; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

options.text: Give flumazenil 0.2 mg IV to reverse the benzodiazepine component of the coingestion
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdoses that may include proconvulsant drugs (TCAs, other antidepressants, cocaine) because seizure control is then lost when benzodiazepine antagonism strips away the sole anticonvulsant; TCA overdose lowers seizure threshold. Would never be correct in TCA co-ingestion (Source: Poisons Information Centre; AMH).

options.text: Give physostigmine 2 mg IV to reverse the anticholinergic component
options.rationale: Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic delirium but is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it precipitates seizures, bradyarrhythmia, and asystole via unopposed cholinergic tone against sodium-channel-blocked myocardium. Would never be correct (Source: Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Give amiodarone 300 mg IV for the sinus tachycardia and QT prolongation
options.rationale: Class III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol) worsen TCA cardiotoxicity by further slowing conduction and prolonging QT; class Ia (procainamide, quinidine) is also contraindicated for the same reason. Would never be correct in TCA overdose (Source: Poisons Information Centre; AMH).

options.text: Give intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent 100 mL bolus as first-line antidote
options.rationale: Intravenous lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy in TCA overdose with cardiovascular collapse or arrest refractory to sodium bicarbonate and standard resuscitation, not first-line for QRS widening with preserved perfusion. Would be reserved for arrest or refractory shock (Source: Poisons Information Centre).

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose produces a fast-sodium-channel blockade that lengthens phase 0 depolarisation, widening the QRS and predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia. It also has anticholinergic (dry, tachycardia, mydriasis), antihistaminergic (sedation), alpha-1 antagonist (hypotension), and central sodium-channel (seizures) effects. Australian toxicology triggers for sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus are QRS above 100 ms, R in aVR above 3 mm, systolic BP below 90, or ventricular arrhythmia; repeat until QRS narrows and pH reaches around 7.45-7.55. Contraindicated agents are flumazenil (proconvulsant reversal), physostigmine (bradyasystole risk), and class Ia and III antiarrhythmics. IV lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiovascular collapse.
key_points: TCA cardiotoxicity = fast sodium channel blockade
Bicarbonate trigger: QRS >100 ms, R in aVR >3 mm, SBP <90, or ventricular arrhythmia
Contraindicated: flumazenil, physostigmine, class Ia and III antiarrhythmics
Lipid emulsion = rescue for refractory shock or arrest
Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26 for all Australian overdose consults
explanation.pearls: In context: sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus is triggered by QRS above 100 ms or an R wave above 3 mm in aVR after TCA overdose; flumazenil, physostigmine and class III antiarrhythmics are all contraindicated (Poisons Information Centre).

subtopic_detail: Discontinuation syndrome pattern and cross-taper strategy
stem: A 42-year-old man on paroxetine 40 mg daily for 4 years for panic disorder felt well and stopped his medication three days ago without tapering. He now describes dizziness on head turning, brief electric-shock sensations down the back of his neck when he moves his eyes, nausea, insomnia with vivid dreams, and irritability. His panic symptoms have not returned. He is otherwise well.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Restart paroxetine 40 mg daily to resolve symptoms, then taper by 10 mg every 2-4 weeks with monitoring for return of panic
options.rationale: This is textbook SSRI discontinuation syndrome (FINISH pattern: Flu-like, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbance, Hyperarousal); paroxetine and venlafaxine are the highest-risk agents because of short half-lives and lack of active metabolite. Restarting the drug promptly relieves symptoms, then a gradual taper over 4-8 weeks or longer is appropriate; the taper rate is individualised to symptom emergence at each step. Some patients require hyperbolic tapers (progressively smaller decrements) at low doses (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH; Australian Prescriber).

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily as a substitute given its long half-life and self-tapering profile
options.rationale: Fluoxetine substitution is an accepted strategy for particularly troublesome discontinuation syndromes because its long half-life allows self-taper, but restart-and-taper of the original drug is first-line; substitution changes the pharmacological target and is reserved for failed tapers. Would be a second-line strategy (Source: Australian Prescriber; AMH).

options.text: Reassure that this represents rebound panic disorder and start pregabalin 75 mg BD
options.rationale: The symptom pattern (electric-shock sensations, imbalance on eye movement, sensory hyperarousal) is characteristic of discontinuation syndrome, not of returning panic disorder; panic recurs as anticipatory anxiety and panic attacks. Would misdirect treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start prochlorperazine 5 mg TDS for vestibular symptoms and diazepam 5 mg nocte for insomnia
options.rationale: Symptomatic treatment does not address the underlying serotonergic withdrawal and prochlorperazine adds antipsychotic risk (EPS, sedation) plus dopamine antagonism that can lower panic threshold; benzodiazepines carry dependence risk in panic disorder. Would never be first-line (Source: AMH).

options.text: Reassure that symptoms will resolve spontaneously within 24 hours and continue observation without pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Discontinuation symptoms typically last 1-3 weeks and can be severe enough to impair function; watchful waiting for a symptomatic patient with a straightforward pharmacological remedy is unnecessary suffering. Would apply only when symptoms were minor and self-limiting within hours (Source: Australian Prescriber).

explanation.summary: Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome follows abrupt cessation or rapid taper of an SSRI or SNRI, typically 1-4 days after the last dose, and lasts 1-3 weeks. The classic FINISH pattern is Flu-like symptoms, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance (dizziness), Sensory disturbance (electric-shock sensations, paraesthesiae worse on eye movement or head turning), and Hyperarousal. Paroxetine and venlafaxine are highest-risk due to short half-lives and no active metabolites; fluoxetine is lowest-risk. Diagnostic discrimination from relapse is important: discontinuation symptoms include sensory/vestibular features not seen in the primary disorder, appear rapidly (days), and resolve quickly when the drug is restarted. Standard taper is over 4-8 weeks; hyperbolic tapers (progressively smaller decrements at low doses) are increasingly used and can extend over months for long-term users.
key_points: FINISH: Flu-like, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbance, Hyperarousal
Onset 1-4 days after cessation; duration 1-3 weeks
Paroxetine and venlafaxine highest-risk (short half-life)
Fluoxetine substitution is second-line for persistent syndrome
Hyperbolic tapers (progressively smaller decrements) at low doses
explanation.pearls: In context: electric-shock sensations, imbalance and hyperarousal within days of stopping paroxetine or venlafaxine is discontinuation syndrome, not relapse; restart and slow taper resolves it (Australian Prescriber; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

subtopic_detail: Switch to aripiprazole for risperidone-induced prolactin rise
stem:
A 26-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been on risperidone 4 mg daily for 18 months with good symptom control. Over the past 6 months she has developed amenorrhoea, milky breast discharge, and reduced libido. She is distressed by these symptoms and by her weight gain of 6 kg since starting treatment. She is sexually active with a same-sex partner and uses no contraception. Beta-hCG is negative and TSH is 2.1 mIU/L.

Prolactin is 1850 mIU/L (normal <500).

data_table.Bloods: Prolactin 1850 mIU/L (<500), beta-hCG negative, TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), LFTs and U&Es within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral galactorrhoea on expression; no visual field defect

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue risperidone and add bromocriptine 2.5 mg BD to lower prolactin
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists risk destabilising psychosis in a patient with schizophrenia and only partially address the pharmacological driver; switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic is preferred as first-line. Bromocriptine is reserved for those in whom switching is contraindicated or ineffective (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cross-taper risperidone to aripiprazole over 4-6 weeks and monitor prolactin, symptoms, and akathisia
options.rationale: Risperidone (with paliperidone and amisulpride) causes dose-dependent prolactin elevation because it is a potent D2 antagonist that penetrates the tuberoinfundibular pathway poorly protected by the blood-brain barrier. Aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist and typically lowers prolactin toward normal, making a switch or add-on the strongest evidence-based intervention for symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia. Akathisia is the main tolerability issue on aripiprazole and warrants monitoring during titration (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Order urgent pituitary MRI for a prolactinoma given the elevated prolactin
options.rationale: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia is the leading cause of drug-induced prolactin rise; a value below 2500 mIU/L in a patient on a known prolactin-elevating antipsychotic without visual field defects or headache is explained by the drug. MRI is warranted only if prolactin remains elevated after switch or exceeds 5000 mIU/L (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Increase risperidone to 6 mg daily and accept prolactin elevation as a class effect
options.rationale: Dose escalation worsens the dose-dependent prolactin rise and the patient is already symptomatic; class-effect framing is incorrect because aripiprazole, quetiapine, olanzapine, clozapine, and lurasidone have lower prolactin liability. Would never be correct (Source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Reduce risperidone to 2 mg daily and add cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly
options.rationale: Dose reduction can help but often at the cost of symptom control, and cabergoline (like bromocriptine) risks psychosis relapse; switching to a prolactin-sparing agent is the primary strategy. Would be second-line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia is a dose-dependent tuberoinfundibular effect of potent D2 antagonists poorly protected by the blood-brain barrier at the median eminence. The worst offenders are risperidone, paliperidone, and amisulpride; haloperidol and other typical antipsychotics also elevate prolactin significantly. Aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist and typically lowers prolactin toward normal. Quetiapine, olanzapine, clozapine, and lurasidone have lower prolactin liability than risperidone. Clinical consequences include amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, gynaecomastia in men, and long-term bone mineral density loss with an increased fracture risk. RANZCP guidance is to switch to a prolactin-sparing agent when hyperprolactinaemia is symptomatic; augmentation with low-dose aripiprazole is an alternative when full switch is not feasible.
key_points: Worst offenders: risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride, haloperidol
Aripiprazole (D2 partial agonist) lowers prolactin toward normal
Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia = switch or add aripiprazole
Dopamine agonist add-on risks destabilising psychosis
Long-term hyperprolactinaemia lowers bone mineral density
explanation.pearls: In context: for symptomatic risperidone-induced hyperprolactinaemia, switch to or augment with aripiprazole (D2 partial agonist) rather than adding a dopamine agonist that risks destabilising psychosis (RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation and rising clozapine trough
stem:
A 45-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 500 mg nocte for six years with steady-state trough level 450 micrograms/L. He is admitted to a general medical ward for community-acquired pneumonia and is placed under smoke-free hospital policy. On day 4 of admission the nursing staff report he has become increasingly drowsy, ataxic, and has had two episodes of hypersalivation with a brief myoclonic jerk.

He smoked 25 cigarettes a day pre-admission and has not smoked since arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 12, SpO2 96%, temperature 37.0
data_table.Bloods: Clozapine trough today 1120 micrograms/L (therapeutic 350-600), norclozapine 260 micrograms/L, ratio 4.3, FBC unchanged, LFTs and U&Es within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 500 mg nocte, amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg BD (day 4)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue clozapine at 500 mg nocte and add sodium valproate 500 mg BD for seizure cover
options.rationale: The clozapine level is more than double therapeutic and the mechanism is loss of tobacco-driven CYP1A2 induction from smoking cessation; adding valproate does not address the pharmacokinetic driver and adds sedation, weight gain, and hepatotoxicity risk. Would be correct only when seizure occurred on a therapeutic level (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Reduce clozapine to approximately 250 mg nocte and offer nicotine replacement therapy (patches plus short-acting), with repeat trough level in 3-5 days
options.rationale: Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2 (via polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, not nicotine); cessation raises clozapine plasma levels by around 50-100 percent within 2-4 weeks and can precipitate toxicity within days. Halving the dose to match the ~50 percent loss of induction, plus NRT to blunt withdrawal, is the AMH/Maudsley recommendation. Nicotine itself does not induce CYP1A2 so NRT does not restore the interaction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Cease clozapine entirely and switch to olanzapine 20 mg nocte to control psychosis
options.rationale: Complete cessation of clozapine risks catastrophic psychotic relapse (>50 percent within 6 months in TRS) and olanzapine has not been shown equivalent for the treatment-resistant illness that clozapine was addressing; dose reduction plus level monitoring is preferred. Would be considered only if clozapine were no longer safe at any dose (Source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines).

options.text: Continue clozapine at current dose and allow him to smoke in a designated area to restore CYP1A2 induction
options.rationale: Australian smoke-free hospital policy does not permit designated smoking areas on hospital grounds; encouraging resumed smoking in a patient who has quit works against long-term cardiovascular and cancer risk goals. NRT plus dose reduction is the correct approach (Source: RACGP smoking cessation; AMH).

options.text: Change antibiotic from amoxicillin-clavulanate to ciprofloxacin to cover atypical pathogens
options.rationale: Ciprofloxacin is a potent CYP1A2 inhibitor and would further increase clozapine levels; it is a well-documented cause of clozapine toxicity and should be actively avoided in clozapine-treated patients. Would be an active harm here (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Clozapine is metabolised primarily by CYP1A2, which is induced by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke (not by nicotine). Smoking cessation removes this induction and clozapine plasma levels rise by 50-100 percent over 2-4 weeks (some patients within days), producing sedation, ataxia, hypersalivation, myoclonus and reduced seizure threshold. The Australian approach on hospital admission is to preemptively halve the clozapine dose in heavy smokers who become smoke-free, offer NRT to manage withdrawal (nicotine does not restore CYP1A2 induction), and check a trough level within 3-5 days. CYP1A2 inhibitors to avoid in clozapine patients include ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine, and caffeine excess. The reverse also holds: a patient who resumes heavy smoking after discharge needs dose re-escalation to avoid subtherapeutic levels and psychotic relapse.
key_points: Tobacco smoke (PAHs) induces CYP1A2; nicotine does not
Smoking cessation raises clozapine level by 50-100 percent in 2-4 weeks
Halve dose plus NRT on smoke-free admission for heavy smokers
Avoid ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine, and caffeine excess (all raise clozapine)
Re-escalate dose on discharge if smoking resumes
explanation.pearls: In context: any heavy smoker admitted on clozapine to a smoke-free hospital needs preemptive dose reduction (roughly half) plus NRT and a trough level in 3-5 days, because tobacco cessation raises the level 50-100 percent (AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

subtopic_detail: Lambert schedule 6-week metabolic review after olanzapine initiation
stem:
A 30-year-old woman started olanzapine 10 mg nocte 6 weeks ago for a first episode of psychosis. Baseline weight, BMI, waist circumference, BP, fasting glucose, fasting lipids, and ECG were all recorded and normal before initiation. She has gained 3.5 kg since starting and reports increased hunger and thirst.

She has no personal or family history of diabetes.

data_table.Examination: Weight 71 kg (baseline 67.5 kg), BMI 25.4 (baseline 24.1), waist 88 cm (baseline 84)

lead_in: Which set of investigations is most appropriate at the 6-week metabolic review under the RANZCP-endorsed Lambert schedule?

options.text: Fasting glucose (or HbA1c), fasting lipids, weight, BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure
options.rationale: The Lambert schedule endorsed by RANZCP mandates the full metabolic panel (fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids, weight, BMI, waist, BP) at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, and annually after initiation of any second-generation antipsychotic; olanzapine and clozapine have the highest metabolic burden and reviewing at 6 weeks captures early weight gain and dysglycaemia. ECG is repeated only for a clinical indication (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia; Australian Prescriber).

options.text: Weight and BMI only; bloods deferred to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Bloods at 6 weeks are part of the Lambert schedule; deferring them misses the highest-yield early window for olanzapine-related dysglycaemia. Would be correct only for a lower-risk antipsychotic outside this schedule (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia).

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, and 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring
options.rationale: OGTT, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR are research-grade metrics not part of the Lambert schedule; ambulatory BP monitoring is not routine. Fasting glucose or HbA1c and clinic BP are sufficient. Would never be routine (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia).

options.text: Prolactin, TSH, and 24-hour urinary cortisol as a hormonal panel
options.rationale: Prolactin monitoring is indicated only for prolactin-elevating antipsychotics (risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride) when symptomatic; TSH and cortisol are not part of the metabolic monitoring schedule. Would misdirect the review (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Repeat ECG and echocardiogram plus troponin and CRP
options.rationale: This cardiac workup is the clozapine myocarditis screen (weekly troponin plus CRP in the first four weeks) not the routine metabolic panel for olanzapine. Would be misdirected (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: The Lambert schedule (endorsed by RANZCP) sets out routine metabolic monitoring for any patient on a second-generation antipsychotic: baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, then annually. At each timepoint the panel is weight, BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose (or HbA1c), and fasting lipids. ECG is at baseline and repeated only for clinical indication or new QT-prolonging medication. Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest metabolic burden; quetiapine and risperidone are intermediate; aripiprazole and lurasidone are lowest. Intervention triggers are sustained weight gain above 7 percent of baseline, new HbA1c above 48 mmol/mol, fasting glucose above 6.1 mmol/L, LDL above 3.5 mmol/L, or metabolic syndrome criteria. Escalation options are lifestyle intervention, metformin (off-label at 1000-2000 mg daily), and switching to a lower-metabolic-burden agent.
key_points: Lambert schedule: baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, then annually
Panel: weight, BMI, waist, BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids
Olanzapine and clozapine highest burden; aripiprazole and lurasidone lowest
Intervention trigger: >7 percent weight gain or new metabolic syndrome criteria
Metformin (off-label) is first-line pharmacological mitigation
explanation.pearls: In context: the Lambert schedule requires a full metabolic panel (weight, BMI, waist, BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids) at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, then annually on any second-generation antipsychotic (RANZCP; Australian Prescriber).

subtopic_detail: Paliperidone palmitate loading regimen with oral overlap
stem:
A 33-year-old man with schizophrenia has had three admissions in two years for non-adherence relapses despite good response to oral paliperidone 6 mg daily. He agrees to a long-acting injectable paliperidone palmitate. He has no allergies and has tolerated oral paliperidone without extrapyramidal symptoms.

He was last dosed with oral paliperidone this morning.

data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&Es, LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: Which paliperidone palmitate initiation regimen is most appropriate under the TGA product information?

options.text: 150 mg IM deltoid on day 1 and 100 mg IM deltoid on day 8, then 75 mg IM monthly maintenance (deltoid or gluteal); no oral overlap required
options.rationale: The TGA-registered paliperidone palmitate loading is 150 mg deltoid on day 1 and 100 mg deltoid on day 8 (both deltoid; site matters for absorption), then monthly maintenance in the range 25-150 mg. The two-injection load rapidly achieves therapeutic plasma levels so oral overlap is not required after the second loading injection. Maintenance dose is chosen based on prior oral dose equivalence (Source: TGA PI Paliperidone Palmitate; AMH; Australian Prescriber).

options.text: Give a single 100 mg gluteal injection and continue oral paliperidone 6 mg daily for 4 weeks as an overlap
options.rationale: Single-dose loading via gluteal injection does not achieve therapeutic plasma levels quickly and requires extended oral overlap, which defeats the adherence rationale for depot; the registered regimen uses two deltoid loading doses. Would never be the standard TGA-registered regimen (Source: TGA PI Paliperidone Palmitate).

options.text: Give paliperidone palmitate 234 mg IM every 4 weeks starting today with no loading and no oral overlap
options.rationale: 234 mg is a dose used in the every-3-month long-acting formulation (Trevicta) which requires prior stabilisation on monthly paliperidone palmitate; using it as monthly initiation gives supratherapeutic levels and skips the loading protocol. Would never be correct as initiation (Source: TGA PI Paliperidone Palmitate).

options.text: Give risperidone long-acting injection 25 mg IM every 2 weeks with oral risperidone overlap for 3 weeks
options.rationale: This is the risperidone LAI regimen (not paliperidone palmitate) which does require 3-week oral overlap because the depot has a lag phase. It also requires a switch of active drug, which is not the goal here. Would apply only when starting risperidone LAI (Source: AMH).

options.text: Give haloperidol decanoate 100 mg IM monthly and cease all paliperidone the same day
options.rationale: Haloperidol decanoate is a first-generation depot with higher EPS risk and is not equivalent to paliperidone; switching antipsychotic class without indication is not appropriate. Would apply only when a change in agent was clinically justified (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Paliperidone palmitate (Invega Sustenna) monthly LAI is TGA-registered with a two-injection deltoid loading protocol: 150 mg day 1 plus 100 mg day 8, then monthly maintenance 25-150 mg. Both loading injections must be given deltoid (not gluteal); the deltoid-versus-gluteal absorption difference is deliberate and product-specific. Oral antipsychotic overlap is not required after the second loading dose. Common maintenance doses translate roughly to oral paliperidone equivalence (75 mg monthly ~ 3 mg daily; 100 mg ~ 6 mg; 150 mg ~ 12 mg). Trevicta (paliperidone palmitate every 3 months) requires prior stabilisation on monthly Sustenna for at least 4 months before switching. Risperidone LAI (Consta) is a different formulation requiring 3-week oral overlap because of a lag phase before therapeutic levels are reached.
key_points: Paliperidone palmitate load: 150 mg deltoid day 1 + 100 mg deltoid day 8
Loading doses must be deltoid, not gluteal
No oral overlap required after second loading dose
Monthly maintenance range 25-150 mg
Trevicta 3-monthly requires prior 4+ months on monthly Sustenna
explanation.pearls: In context: the TGA-registered paliperidone palmitate load is 150 mg deltoid on day 1 and 100 mg deltoid on day 8 with no oral overlap; risperidone LAI still requires 3-week oral overlap because it has a lag phase (TGA PI; AMH).
